course.title: Logic and Reasoning
course.description: Work out what follows from what. Read arguments carefully, test them against cases, and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong.
course.audience: A general reader with no background in formal logic who wants to argue and evaluate arguments more carefully.

paragraphs: How can you tell whether a conclusion really follows from the reasons given for it? Logic is the study of that question, and it gives you ways of answering it that don't depend on how convincing an argument sounds. It helps you read arguments more carefully and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong, and it is also the rule-following side of mathematics and computing.

The course has eight lessons in two parts. The first, Deduction, begins with the sentences logic works on, then takes up if-then claims, the ways of turning one round, a puzzle solved by trying each case, and the truth table, which lists every case at once. The second, Arguments, finds the conclusion and the reasons in an argument in everyday words, separates whether the conclusion follows from whether the reasons are true, and names the common ways reasoning fails.
Each lesson tells you the idea first and asks questions afterwards, so you meet a question only once you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a claim from a question or a command, and say what its truth value is.
You'll be able to say exactly when an if-then rule is broken, and write its converse and its contrapositive.
You'll be able to solve a knights and knaves puzzle by trying each case and ruling out the ones that break a rule.
You'll be able to build a truth table for two claims and use it to test a piece of reasoning.
You'll be able to pick out the conclusion of an argument, tell valid from sound, and name the common fallacies.
introduction.prerequisites: You don't need any background in logic or mathematics, only the habit of reading a sentence carefully.

lessons.title: What logic operates on

steps.headline: A claim is a sentence that can turn out to be wrong

lead.text: Sort the sentences you meet by what they are doing and three kinds come out. Some say how things are, such as “The lamp is on” or “The door is locked”. Some ask, as in “Is the door locked?”, and some tell, as in “Switch the lamp on”. We call a sentence of the first kind a **claim**, and the test for one is whether it can be *wrong*.

afterFigure.text: A question isn't wrong when you answer it, it is simply answered, and a command isn't wrong either, since it is obeyed or ignored. Only a claim puts forward **something the world can contradict**, and that is why logic, which is about what follows from what we put forward, works on claims and leaves the other two kinds alone.
Notice that the test has nothing to do with whether we agree or can check. “The lamp is on” is a claim whether or not the lamp is on, and whether or not you can see it from where you are.

steps.headline: A claim is true or false, whether or not anyone knows which

lead.text: Go back to the sealed envelope. The sentence “The envelope holds a £10 note” hasn't been checked, but that doesn't leave it in some third state of being neither right nor wrong. The envelope holds a note or it doesn't, and whichever it is has already settled the sentence. Open the envelope each way in the figure and see what happens to it, and to its opposite, “The envelope holds no £10 note”.

afterFigure.text: Whichever way the envelope goes, one sentence is true and the other false. We call *true* or *false* a claim's **truth value**, and in this course every claim has exactly one of the two. “Unknown” is not a third value, because it describes you, who haven't looked, and not the sentence.

The same goes for a claim about the past that no one can now check, or about the number of sweets in a jar that nobody has counted. In every such case **the facts fix the truth value**, and whether we have found it out is a separate matter.

steps.headline: The negation of a claim says the opposite, and takes the opposite truth value

lead.text: The two sentences in the envelope figure are linked in a way that is worth naming. “The envelope holds no £10 note” says exactly what you would need to say to deny the first, and we call a claim that denies another claim its **negation**. We write the negation of a claim p as ¬p, read “not p”, so if p is “The lamp is on”, then ¬p is “The lamp is not on”.

Because ¬p is true exactly when p is false, negating a claim reverses its truth value: **if p is true then ¬p is false, and if p is false then ¬p is true**. The two can never share a value, and negating twice puts you back where you began.

afterFigure.text: Take care that a negation denies the claim and nothing more. The negation of “The soup is hot” is “The soup is not hot”, which leaves room for the soup being merely warm, and it is *not* “The soup is cold”.

lead.text: Here p is the claim “The lamp is on”, and we are told that it is true.

reveal.text: Each row of the table sets a value of p beside the value of ¬p, and in both rows the two differ.

steps.headline: A claim that people dispute is still a claim

lead.text: So far the claims have been ones you could settle by looking. Many sentences that people argue over are not like that, such as “Cats make better pets than dogs” or “The new tax is unfair”. It is tempting to say that these are only opinions, neither true nor false, and so none of logic's business.

But look at what the speaker is doing. Someone who says the tax is unfair is putting something forward as *how things are*, and someone who answers “No, it isn't” is contradicting it, which is exactly what claims allow and questions and commands do not. **Being a claim doesn't depend on our agreeing, or even on our knowing how to settle it**; it depends only on the sentence being put forward as true, so that it can be doubted.

Whether some claims, about beauty or fairness for example, have a truth value at all is a hard question in philosophy, and we can leave it open. Logic doesn't need the answer, because it asks what follows *if* the claim is true and what follows if it is false.
Here is a sentence people really do disagree about.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence: “The envelope on the table holds a £10 note.” The envelope is sealed and nobody has looked inside, so we can't say whether the sentence is right. We can say something else about it, though, that we couldn't say about “Does the envelope hold a £10 note?” or “Open the envelope.” The first sentence will be shown to be right or wrong the moment someone looks, and neither of the other two ever will be.

That difference is what this whole course rests on. Logic works on sentences that can be *right or wrong*, and asks what follows when they are, so before we can do anything else we need to pick those sentences out, and to see why not knowing the answer doesn't change what kind of sentence we have.

blocks.text: A **claim** says how things are, so unlike a question or a command it can turn out to be wrong, even when people dispute it. Each claim has one of two **truth values**, true or false, and the facts settle which *whether or not* anyone has looked. Its **negation**, ¬p, says the opposite, and so always takes the other value.

lessons.title: If-then claims

steps.headline: An if-then claim joins a condition to a result

lead.text: Look again at the lock's rule: “If the access code is correct, the door opens.” It is built out of two shorter [[claims|Sentences that say how things are, so they can turn out to be wrong. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]], “The access code is correct” and “The door opens”, joined so that the first is offered as a reason for the second. We call a claim built this way a **conditional**. The part after “if” is its **antecedent**, the part after “then” is its **consequent**, and if we let p stand for the first and q for the second we can write the whole thing as p → q, read “if p then q”.

afterFigure.text: The arrow is a fair picture of what a conditional does: it points *from* the condition *to* what is said to follow. One thing to watch is that the “then” is often dropped and the order often swapped. “The door opens if the code is correct” says exactly what the lock's rule says, and its antecedent is still the code, because **the antecedent is whatever follows “if”**, wherever it stands in the sentence.

diagram.alt: Two boxes joined by an arrow. The left box is p, the antecedent: the access code is correct. The right box is q, the consequent: the door opens. Together they read p → q.
diagram.caption: The rule as a conditional: the arrow points from the condition to what is said to follow.

steps.headline: A conditional is put to the test only when its condition holds

lead.text: When can we say that a rule like this has failed? Take the two things that can happen once the code has been entered correctly. If the door opens, the rule has done its job. If the door stays shut, the rule has been broken, and the claim “If the code is correct, the door opens” is *false*. The figure sets the two side by side, and in both the code is right, so the only difference is what the door does.

afterFigure.text: So a conditional is false when **its antecedent is true and its consequent is false**, because that is a case where the rule demands something and doesn't get it. The remaining cases are less obvious, and the next screens go through them.

reveal.text: The table lists all four combinations of p and q, and only the second row, with p true and q false, is one where p → q comes out false.

lead.text: Now for the cases where the code is wrong. Suppose it is, and the door stays shut, so that p and q are both false.

reveal.text: The rule said what happens when the code is correct and nothing else, so a shut door after a wrong code contradicts nothing it said.

steps.headline: A conditional says nothing about what happens when its antecedent is false

lead.text: The pull to call that case false is strong, and it comes from reading the rule as a claim about the door in general. It isn't one. “If the code is correct, the door opens” tells us what happens in one situation, when the code is right, and it stays quiet about every other. With a wrong code the door can stay shut, as we would expect, or it can open because someone inside presses the release button, and neither contradicts what the rule says. The figure shows both.

afterFigure.text: In both pictures the antecedent is false, so the rule was never put to the test. Nothing has broken it, and we count the conditional as **true whenever its antecedent is false**, whatever the consequent does. That is a convention, but it is the right one for a rule: a rule that hasn't been broken has been kept, and the conditional stays a claim with a definite [[truth value|True or false: the one verdict a claim has. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]].

If the lock were also meant to open the door *only* for the right code, that would be a second rule, “if the door opens, the code is correct”. It is a different claim, and the next lesson is about how it differs.

steps.headline: Four cases, and only one of them breaks a conditional

lead.text: Put the four cases in one list and the whole behaviour of p → q is on the page. Each of p and q can be true or false, which gives four combinations, and the conditional is false in exactly one of them, where p is true and q is false. A list of this kind, which sets out every case and the value the claim takes in each, is called a **truth table**, and we'll build our own in lesson five.

afterFigure.text: The table shows why a conditional says less than it seems to. It never asserts that p is true, and it doesn't assert that p *causes* q, only that p without q is ruled out. Whenever you meet an if-then claim, **look for the one case it forbids**, and expect everything else to be left open.

lessons.nextAction: Next, what happens when an if-then claim is turned round.

blocks.text: A lock on a door comes with a rule: if the access code is correct, the door opens. Suppose someone types the right code and the door stays shut. Plainly the rule has failed. Now suppose someone types the *wrong* code and the door opens anyway, because a person inside has pressed the release button. Has the rule failed then?

Most people say that it has, since the door has done something the code didn't entitle it to do, and most people are wrong. The rule says what must happen when the code is right and says nothing about what happens when it is wrong. Working out exactly what an if-then claim does and doesn't say is worth the effort, because a great many of the arguments we meet are built out of if-then claims.

intro.whyItMatters: Most rules, laws and arguments are if-then claims, and most mistakes about them come from misreading when they fail.

recap.keyIdea: A conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false, and true in every other case.

blocks.text: An **if-then claim** joins an antecedent p to a consequent q, and the arrow points from the condition to what is said to follow. It forbids exactly *one* case, p true with q false, so it is true in the other three, including both in which p is false, because a rule whose condition never arises has not been broken.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn a conditional round, and find that one way of doing it changes what it says and another doesn't.

lessons.title: Converse and contrapositive

steps.headline: Swapping the two parts of a conditional gives a new claim, its converse

lead.text: Start with the lock's [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in 'If-then claims'.]], p → q, where p is “The code is correct” and q is “The door opens”. The simplest way to turn a rule round is to swap its [[antecedent|The part of a conditional after “if”: the condition. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] and its [[consequent|The part of a conditional after “then”: what is said to follow. Met in 'If-then claims'.]], which gives q → p, or in words “If the door opens, the code is correct”. We call the claim we get by swapping the two parts the **converse** of the original, and the figure sets the two side by side.

afterFigure.text: Notice what the swap leaves alone. Nothing is negated, and each part is the very claim it was before, so the converse is made of *exactly the same material* as the original. It is easy to hear it as just another way of saying the same thing, because the words are so close, but we can't tell by listening. **Whether two conditionals say the same thing has to be checked case by case**, as we did for the conditional itself.

diagram.alt: Two diagrams of a rule. In the first, p (the code is correct) points to q (the door opens). In the second the halves are swapped, so q points to p, and this is the converse.
diagram.caption: The rule, and the claim made by swapping its two halves. The swapped claim is the converse.

steps.headline: Two claims are the same only if they take the same truth value in every case

lead.text: How do we decide whether two claims say the same thing? Not by how alike their wording is, but by whether they can *ever* disagree. If there is a case in which one is true and the other false, they are different claims, and if there is no such case, they are the same as far as logic is concerned. So we check them one case at a time. The figure begins the check for p → q and its converse q → p, with a row for each combination of p and q, and in the first row, where both are true, p → q is true and so is q → p.

afterFigure.text: One row of agreement settles nothing, because two quite different claims can agree in some rows. **One row of disagreement settles everything**, because it shows that the two can come apart. We should therefore go looking for such a row, and the natural place to start is where p and q have different values.

diagram.caption: To compare two claims, check them row by row. The first row is done, and the two agree in it.

lead.text: Take the row in which p is false and q is true: the code is wrong, and the door opens anyway. We know what the conditional p → q does there. What does the converse do?

reveal.text: In this row q → p is false, while p → q is true because its antecedent is false. The two disagree, so the converse is a *different* claim from the original.

steps.headline: Swapping the parts and negating both gives a second rule, the contrapositive

lead.text: There is another way to turn the rule round. Swap the parts as before, and then [[negate|To make the claim that denies another, written ¬p. It reverses the truth value. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]] each of them, so that “The code is correct” becomes “The code is not correct”, and “The door opens” becomes “The door does not open”. The result is ¬q → ¬p, read “if not q then not p”, which in words is “If the door does not open, the code is not correct”. We call it the **contrapositive** of p → q.

afterFigure.text: *Both* steps are needed. Swapping without negating gives the [[converse|The conditional with its parts swapped: q → p. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and negating without swapping gives ¬p → ¬q, “If the code is not correct, the door does not open”, which is neither of the others. The contrapositive is the one that **swaps and negates**.

steps.headline: Does the contrapositive ever disagree with the original?

lead.text: The rows will tell us. For each combination of p and q we work out p → q first and ¬q → ¬p second, and the values are written in that order.

workedSteps.text: Take p true and q true. Then p → q is true. In the contrapositive ¬q is false, so its antecedent is false and ¬q → ¬p is true as well.

Take p true and q false. Now p → q has a true antecedent and a false consequent, so it is false. In the contrapositive ¬q is true and ¬p is false, so it has a true antecedent and a false consequent too.
Take p false and q true. Then p → q is true, because its antecedent is false. Here ¬q is false, so the contrapositive's antecedent is false and it is true too.
Take p false and q false. Then p → q is true. Now ¬q and ¬p are both true, so ¬q → ¬p has a true antecedent and a true consequent, and it is true.
In all four rows the two claims take the same value, so there is no case in which they can disagree. The contrapositive says the same thing as the original.

lead.text: The worked example compared the two claims one row at a time. A count of the disagreements puts the result in a single number.

steps.headline: A rule can be used backwards through its contrapositive, never through its converse

lead.text: The practical gain is that the contrapositive gives us a second way of using a rule we already hold. Because “If the code is correct, the door opens” and “If the door does not open, the code is not correct” say the same thing, we may take the rule together with a door that stayed shut and conclude that the code was wrong. The conclusion is exactly as safe as the rule itself.

The converse offers no such service. From an open door we would like to say that the code was right, but that needs the rule “If the door opens, the code is correct”, which the manual *never* gave us and which, as the release button showed, can be false while the manual's rule is true. So from the original rule and an open door **nothing follows about the code**. When you want to use a rule backwards, swap its parts and negate both, and be suspicious of any argument that swaps alone.
Here is the contrapositive on a new rule.

lessons.orientation: The converse and the contrapositive of an if-then claim, and which one says the same as the original.
lessons.nextAction: Next, a puzzle solved by trying each case in turn.

blocks.text: Suppose a lock's manual says: if the access code is correct, the door opens. Two people reason from it. One says that the door didn't open, so the code can't have been correct. The other says that the door did open, so the code must have been correct. The two arguments look as alike as can be, yet the second is unsafe, because a person inside can open the door with the release button whatever code was typed, while the first seems to leave no room for doubt.

What separates them is the way each one turns the rule round. An if-then claim can be turned round in more than one way, and some of the ways give back the same claim in other words while others give a different claim altogether. So which turnings give back the same claim, and which give a different one?

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the converse and contrapositive of an if-then claim, and say which one means the same as the original.
intro.whyItMatters: Reasoning from a rule in the wrong direction is one of the commonest errors in argument, and turning the rule round correctly avoids it.

recap.keyIdea: Swapping a conditional's parts gives its converse, which can disagree with it; swapping and negating both gives its contrapositive, which always agrees.

blocks.text: The **converse** of p → q is q → p, and it is a different claim, since the two split in two of the four cases. The **contrapositive**, ¬q → ¬p, swaps the parts *and* negates both, and it takes the same value as the original in every case, so a rule can be used backwards through its contrapositive but never through its converse.

recap.nextHook: Next we use these ideas on a puzzle in which every speaker either always tells the truth or never does.

lessons.title: Knights and knaves

steps.headline: A knight says only true things and a knave says only false ones

lead.text: On the island in these puzzles everyone is one of two kinds. A **knight** always tells the truth, so every sentence a knight says is true, and a **knave** always lies, so every sentence a knave says is false. You can't tell which kind a person is by looking, which means that everything you learn has to come from what they say.

afterFigure.text: The rule works in both directions, and that is what makes the puzzles solvable. If we know someone is a knight, we know that what they said is true, and if we know that what they said is false, we know they can't be a knight, so they must be a knave. The rule is about the [[truth value|True or false: the one verdict a claim has. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]] of what is said, so a knave may say something long and complicated, as long as it *comes out false*.

steps.headline: To use a statement, assume what its speaker is and follow the consequences

lead.text: Suppose an islander called Cleo says of another, Dan, “Dan is a knight.” We don't know what Cleo is, so we try each possibility in turn and see what it forces. If Cleo is a knight, her sentence is true, so Dan is a knight, and nothing has gone wrong. If Cleo is a knave, her sentence is false, so Dan is not a knight and must be a knave, and again nothing has gone wrong. The figure follows each assumption along its arrows.

afterFigure.text: Neither assumption breaks a rule, so Cleo's sentence doesn't settle *what* she is. What it does settle is *how* she and Dan are related, since in both cases they are the same kind. That is the usual shape of these puzzles: **one statement narrows the possibilities without picking one**, and the work lies in combining statements until a single possibility is left.

steps.headline: List every assignment, and rule out each one that makes someone break their rule

lead.text: The assume-and-follow move can be organised so that nothing is missed. With two islanders, each a knight or a knave, there are four ways the island might be arranged: both knights, both knaves, and the two mixed pairs. We call a choice of kind for every person an **assignment**, and the plan is to write all of them down and test each against what has been said. Take Cleo's sentence again, “Dan is a knight”, and put it to each assignment.

afterFigure.text: Two assignments fail. Where Cleo is a knight and Dan a knave, the knight has said something *false*, and where Cleo is a knave and Dan a knight, the knave has said something *true*. Each of these needs a sentence to be true and false at once, and a situation like that is a **contradiction**, so we rule the assignment out. What is left, an assignment in which nobody breaks the rule for their kind, is a possible answer, and **a puzzle is solved when exactly one assignment is left**.

lead.text: Now put the list to work on Ada's sentence from a moment ago, “Ben is a knave”, and the four assignments for Ada and Ben.

reveal.text: Her sentence fits when she and Ben are of different kinds: Ada a knight and Ben a knave, or Ada a knave and Ben a knight. The other two assignments each make her break the rule for her kind.

steps.headline: Eli says “Fay and I are the same kind”, and Fay says “Eli is a knave”

lead.text: Here is a puzzle solved in full, with every assignment tested against both statements.

workedSteps.text: Four assignments are possible for (Eli, Fay), and we test each against both statements.
Knight–knight: Eli's sentence is true, since they are the same kind. But Fay, a knight, says that Eli is a knave, which is false. A knight has said something false, so this is a contradiction.
Knight–knave: Eli, a knight, says they are the same kind, but they differ, so his sentence is false. A knight has said something false.
Knave–knave: they are the same kind, so Eli's sentence is true, and Eli is a knave.
Knave–knight: Eli is a knave and his sentence is false, as it must be, because the two differ. Fay is a knight and her sentence, “Eli is a knave”, is true. Nobody breaks a rule.
Exactly one assignment is left, so it is the answer.
workedSteps.math: Eli is a knave and Fay is a knight

lead.text: Here is a puzzle for you to solve with the same list. Ada says, “Ben is a knave,” and Ben says, “Ada and I are the same kind.”

reveal.text: Ada's sentence leaves two assignments: Ada a knight and Ben a knave, or Ada a knave and Ben a knight. Ben's sentence rules out the second, because there Ben would be a knight saying they are the same kind when they differ.

steps.headline: Sometimes every assignment is ruled out, and that is an answer too

lead.text: Sometimes the list ends up empty. Suppose an islander says, “I am a knave.” If she is a knight, her sentence is true, so she is a knave, which is a [[contradiction|A case that forces a claim to be both true and false, so it is ruled out. Met earlier in this lesson.]] with her being a knight. If she is a knave, her sentence is true, since she is one, and a knave never says anything true. Either way something goes wrong, and no assignment survives.

What this tells us is that *nobody* on the island can say that sentence. A puzzle that leaves nothing standing hasn't defeated the method, because **an empty list is the correct answer**: the statements cannot all have been made by knights and knaves. The same move, assuming something and showing that it leads to a contradiction, is how mathematicians show that a thing is impossible.
Here is a pair of statements to test in the same way. Cara says, “Drew is a knight,” and Drew says, “Cara is a knave.”

lessons.orientation: Solving a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it until something breaks.
lessons.nextAction: Next, truth tables, which list every case at once.

blocks.text: Imagine an island where everyone either always tells the truth or always lies, and you can't tell which by looking. A woman tells you, “I always tell the truth.” What is she? Someone who always tells the truth would say that, truthfully, and so would someone who always lies, falsely, so the sentence tells you nothing at all.

Change the sentence. Suppose she says of the man beside her, “He always lies.” Now something can be worked out, though perhaps not everything, and what a second person says in turn may settle the rest. The method for working it out is to suppose something and follow it until it either holds up or breaks, which is the move mathematicians use in proofs, and these islanders give us a small place to learn it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll solve a small knights and knaves puzzle by trying each case and ruling out the ones that break a rule.
intro.whyItMatters: Supposing a case and following it until something breaks is how mathematicians prove things, and it works on any argument.

recap.keyIdea: To solve a knights and knaves puzzle, list every assignment, rule out each one that makes someone break the rule for their kind, and see what is left.

blocks.text: A **knight** says only true things and a **knave** only false ones, so each statement can be tested against each **assignment** of kinds. An assignment that makes a knight say something false, or a knave something true, ends in a **contradiction** and is ruled out. The puzzle is solved when exactly one assignment survives, and if none does, the statements could not all have been made, which is an answer in itself.

lessons.title: Building a truth table

steps.headline: A truth table lists every state the claims can be in, one row for each

lead.text: Each lamp is either on or off, so the hallway can be in several different states, and we want each one listed exactly once. Let p be “Lamp 1 is on” and q be “Lamp 2 is on”. We make a column for each claim and a row for each state, and we take the states in a fixed order, with p changing slowest, so that none is missed or counted twice. The last column holds the verdict of the notice, the [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] “If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on”, in each state.

afterFigure.text: A table of this kind, with a row for every combination of true and false and a column for the value of a sentence, is a **truth table**. Reading the last column with the rule from the lesson on if-then claims, the notice is broken in *exactly one* row, the one in which lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is off. **Every possible state is in the table**, so we can be sure that no other state breaks the notice.

diagram.outputLabel: If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on

lead.text: The table is only as complete as its list of rows, so it helps to be able to say in advance how long the list will be.

steps.headline: Each row fixes the value of a sentence built from p and q

lead.text: The last column is what a truth table is for. In each row p and q have definite values, and a sentence made from them has a value that depends on nothing else. We have done this for the conditional. Another common way of joining two claims is with “and”, which we write as ∧, so that p ∧ q reads “p and q”. It asks for *both* claims at once, so **p ∧ q is true in a row only when p is true and q is true there**, and it is false in every other row.

Notice that we never needed to know what p and q were about. Lamps, doors or the weather would give the same column, because the rule for ∧ looks only at the truth values in the row, and that is why one table can serve for every pair of claims.
Here is the table for p ∧ q with its last column hidden. Work out each row before you answer.

reveal.text: Only the first row, with p and q both true, gives “p and q” a true value. In each of the other three rows at least one of the two claims fails, and that is enough to make it false.

steps.headline: In logic, “or” is true when at least one claim is true, even if both are

lead.text: The word “or” needs more care than “and”, because everyday speech uses it in two ways. A sign that offers “tea or coffee” would not be broken by someone who took both, whereas a menu offering “soup or salad” is usually meant to rule out taking both. The first reading, in which both is allowed, is called the **inclusive or**, and the second, in which both is ruled out, is the exclusive or. The figure compares them, and they differ in *only* one row, the one where both are taken.

afterFigure.text: Logic fixes on the inclusive reading and writes it ∨, so that p ∨ q is true in every row where at least one of p and q is true, and **false only when both are false**. If the exclusive meaning is intended, we say so in so many words, as in “p or q but not both”. Choosing one fixed meaning matters because a table has to give one definite value in each row.

reveal.text: The only row that fails is the last, with p and q both false. The row with both true counts, because the inclusive “or” is satisfied by at least one claim and so by two.

steps.headline: A table can test reasoning: keep the rows that fit the facts, and see what holds in all of them

lead.text: Each row of a table is one way the world might be, and that gives us a way to test a piece of reasoning. We are told some facts, and we want to know whether a conclusion must hold. Every fact rules out the rows in which it is false, so we cross those out and keep only the rows that fit everything we know. The figure steps through an example in which we are told that “p and q” is false, and then that p is true.

afterFigure.text: Once the facts have done their work, the rows still standing are all the ways the world could be, given what we know. **A conclusion follows only if it is true in every one of them**, and if even a *single* surviving row makes it false, then the facts do not force it. In the example one row is left, with q false, so q must be false.

steps.headline: Given p or q, and that p is false, must q be true?

lead.text: Here is the table method used on a small argument, with the facts applied one at a time.

workedSteps.text: We are told that p ∨ q is true and that p is false, and we ask whether q must be true. Write each row with p's value first, so that TF means p true and q false, and begin with all four.
The first fact is that p ∨ q is true. It is false only when both claims are false, so the last row goes and the other three stay.
The second fact is that p is false, so every row in which p is true must go.
One row is left, and in it q is true. No row that fits the facts has q false, so the conclusion follows.

lead.text: Now turn the method on a piece of reasoning that sounds sensible but fails. Someone says: “p or q is true, and p is true, so q must be false.”

blocks.text: A hallway has two lamps, and a notice says: if lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on. You can check whether the notice is being obeyed by walking down the hallway and looking, but suppose you want to know in advance what it permits. You would have to work out in which states of the two lamps the notice is broken, and to do that you would need a list of every state the lamps could be in, with the notice's verdict beside each.

A list of that kind is the most reliable tool in this course, because it turns a question about any two claims into a matter of looking things up. It also lets us test a piece of reasoning, by asking whether any state of the world fits the facts we were given and yet contradicts the conclusion someone has drawn from them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll list every case for two claims, work out “and” and “or” in each row, and test reasoning by the rows.
intro.whyItMatters: A table of every case leaves nothing to judgment, so it settles whether a conclusion follows and shows where it fails.

recap.keyIdea: A truth table lists every case for the claims involved, and the rows that fit the known facts decide whether a conclusion follows.

blocks.text: A **truth table** has a row for every combination of true and false, so two claims need four rows and each further claim doubles them. In each row the value of a sentence such as p ∧ q, true only when both hold, or the inclusive p ∨ q, false only when both fail, depends on that row alone. To test reasoning we keep the rows that fit the facts, and the conclusion follows *only if* it holds in every one of them.

lessons.title: Finding the conclusion

steps.headline: The conclusion is the claim being supported, and the premises are the reasons offered for it

lead.text: A speaker who gives reasons is doing something different from one who simply states things. One [[claim|A sentence that says how things are, so it can turn out to be wrong. Met in 'What logic operates on'.]] is set apart as the one the speaker wants you to accept, and the others are offered to get you there. We call the claim to be accepted the **conclusion**, each claim offered in support of it a **premise**, and a conclusion together with its premises an **argument**. In the ferry example the conclusion is that the ferry won't run, and the premises are that the wind is above gale force and that the company cancels the ferry in a gale.

afterFigure.text: The word “argument” does not mean a quarrel here. It means reasons offered for a claim, and it says nothing yet about whether the reasons are any good. A premise is not necessarily true either; it is simply what is *offered*. Whether the premises are true, and whether they support the conclusion, are two further questions that the next lesson takes up. **Finding the conclusion comes first**, because every other question about an argument depends on knowing what it is supposed to show.

steps.headline: Words like “so” and “because” are clues to the roles, not proof of them

lead.text: Speakers often leave signals about which claim is which. Words such as “so”, “therefore”, “thus” and “hence” usually introduce a conclusion, and words such as “because”, “since” and “for” usually introduce a premise. We call them **indicator words**, and in the ferry example the “because” tells us that what follows it is a reason.

They are clues and no more. “Since” can also mean “from the time that”, as in “It has rained since Monday”, where nothing is being supported, and plenty of arguments contain no indicator word at all. When the words don't settle it, ask the question that never fails: *which claim is the speaker trying to get me to accept, and which are there to help?* You can check an answer by adding the word that fits. If “so” reads naturally in front of a claim, it is probably the conclusion.
Here is an argument that follows the usual order: “If the battery is charged, the torch lights. The battery is charged. Therefore the torch lights.”

reveal.text: The first two sentences are the support, and “therefore” introduces what they are meant to establish.

steps.headline: A claim's place in the passage does not decide its role

lead.text: It is natural to expect the conclusion to come last, because that is where we put it when we prove something. In ordinary speech it comes *wherever* the speaker finds convenient. A speaker will often begin with what they want you to accept and give the reasons afterwards, as in “You should take an umbrella. The forecast says rain, and you will be outside all afternoon.”

That passage has no indicator word, and its conclusion is the first sentence. We found it by asking what the other sentences are there to support, and that is the test to trust: **ask what each claim is doing for the others**. A conclusion can come first, last or in the middle, and the same goes for each premise.

steps.headline: “We must leave now, because the station is a long walk away and the last train is at nine”

lead.text: Here is a passage in which the conclusion comes first and a premise comes last, worked from the question of what each claim is doing.

workedSteps.text: Begin with what the speaker wants you to accept. Of the three claims, one tells us what to do, and the other two are facts of the kind that might explain why.

The station being a long walk away and the last train leaving at nine do not ask anything of us. They are offered so that we will see why we must leave, which makes them premises, even though the last of them stands at the end of the passage.
workedSteps.math: Premises: the station is a long walk away; the last train is at nine

workedSteps.text: Check by putting “so” in the right place: the station is a long walk away and the last train is at nine, so we must leave now. It reads naturally, and the other order would not.

lead.text: Now a passage in which a conclusion comes first and the reasons follow, without the help of a “therefore”.

steps.headline: In letters, an argument shows its shape, and a truth table shows when its premises all hold

lead.text: Once the conclusion and premises are found, we can write an argument with the subject matter taken out. Let p be “The battery is charged” and q be “The torch lights”. The torch argument becomes the [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in 'If-then claims'.]] p → q, and p, and therefore q: **two premises and a conclusion**, with nothing about batteries left in it. The figure sets it out.

afterFigure.text: The letters matter because a [[truth table|A list of every case the claims can be in, one row each, with the value of a sentence in each. Met in 'Building a truth table'.]] is then ready to use. Each row is a way the world might be, so the rows in which *every premise is true* are the cases where all of the speaker's reasons hold. A row in which even one premise fails is not one the speaker is asking us to consider. Finding those rows is the first step in testing an argument, and the next lesson shows what to look for in them.

blocks.text: Someone tells you: “The ferry won't run today, because the wind is above gale force and the company cancels the ferry in a gale.” Three claims are joined here, and they are not doing the same job. One of them is the claim the speaker wants you to accept, and the other two are there to persuade you of it.

Which is which? The answer does not lie in the order, since the claim to be accepted came first, nor in how sure any of the three sounds. It lies in what each claim is doing for the others, and seeing that is the first skill of reading someone's reasoning. It has to come before we can ask whether the reasoning is any good, because until we know what is being supported there is nothing to assess.

intro.promise: By the end you'll pick out an argument's conclusion however it is worded, and find the rows where its premises all hold.
intro.whyItMatters: You can't ask whether an argument is any good until you know what it is trying to prove.

recap.keyIdea: The conclusion is the claim an argument wants you to accept, and its premises are the claims offered to support it, whatever order they come in.

blocks.text: An **argument** is a **conclusion** together with the **premises** offered in support of it. Words like “so” and “because” are useful clues but not proof, and a claim's position tells us nothing, so the test is to ask which claim the others are *there to support*. Written in letters, the torch argument shows how a truth table can find the rows in which every premise is true.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask whether the premises of an argument really do support its conclusion, and, separately, whether they are true.

lessons.title: Valid but untrue

steps.headline: An argument is valid when its conclusion has to be true if its premises are

lead.text: The first question a logician asks about an argument is not whether its [[premises|Claims offered in support of a conclusion. Met in 'Finding the conclusion'.]] are true but whether its [[conclusion|The claim an argument wants you to accept. Met in 'Finding the conclusion'.]] *follows* from them. To find out, grant the premises of the whale argument for a moment: suppose that every mammal lives on land, and that whales are mammals. Could whales then live anywhere else? They couldn't, since a whale would be a mammal and every mammal would live on land. When the conclusion is forced in this way we call the argument **valid**: there is no way for all of its premises to be true while its conclusion is false.

afterFigure.text: Validity is a claim about how the premises and the conclusion are *connected*, and it says nothing about whether any of them is true. That is why we could judge the whale argument without knowing anything about whales, and why a valid argument can have a false premise and a false conclusion, as this one does. The reverse holds too: an argument whose premises and conclusion all happen to be true is not thereby valid, because **validity asks what must be so, not what happens to be so**.

lead.text: Take the definition at its word.

steps.headline: To test an argument, look at the rows in which every premise is true

lead.text: We can make that test mechanical with [[truth tables|Lists of every case the claims can be in, one row each, with the value of a sentence in each. Met in 'Building a truth table'.]]. Strip the argument down to letters, so that the particular claims no longer matter, and what remains is its **pattern**. The rows of a table are all the ways the claims might come out, so a pattern is valid exactly when its conclusion is **true in every row in which all its premises are true**. Take the pattern “p ∧ q; therefore q”. The only row in which its premise is true is the first, with p and q both true, and q is true there, so the pattern is valid.

afterFigure.text: Notice that we never asked whether p or q is true *in fact*. We looked only at the rows where the premises are true, and asked whether the conclusion could be false in any of them. If it can't, then no circumstances at all can pull the premises and the conclusion apart. A valid pattern also works whatever claims are put in place of the letters, which is why we can test the pattern once and trust every argument that has its shape.

lead.text: Here is the pattern from the torch argument of the last lesson: “p → q; p; therefore q”. Run the test on it.

reveal.text: The only row in which both premises are true is the first, with p and q both true, and q is true there. No row has true premises and a false conclusion.

steps.headline: One row with true premises and a false conclusion shows that an argument is invalid

lead.text: Now the other side of the test. Suppose some row makes every premise true and the conclusion false. That row is a way things could be in which all the reasons hold and the claim they are meant to support fails, and we call it a **counterexample** to the argument. An argument that has a counterexample is invalid, which just means that it is not valid.

One counterexample is *enough*, because validity is a promise about *every* case, and a single exception breaks it. No number of rows in which the conclusion does come out true can rescue a pattern that has a counterexample somewhere. So while you are testing you can stop the moment you find such a row, whereas you can only call the pattern valid after **every** row with true premises has been checked.

steps.headline: Testing “p ∨ q; q; therefore p”

lead.text: Here is a pattern that has the look of good reasoning, tested row by row.

workedSteps.text: Write the four rows, with p's value first, so that TF means p true and q false.
Keep the rows in which both premises are true. The premise p ∨ q fails only in the last row, and the premise q fails in the second and the last, so two rows remain.
Now look at the conclusion, p, in each of those rows. It is true in TT but false in FT, so FT has true premises and a false conclusion. That row is a counterexample.
The pattern is invalid, however well it seems to behave in the other rows.

lead.text: Now a pattern with a familiar ring: it turns the [[converse|The conditional with its parts swapped: q → p. Met in 'Converse and contrapositive'.]] round. The pattern is “p → q; q; therefore p”.

reveal.text: In the row with p false and q true, p → q is true because its antecedent is false, q is true, and the conclusion p is false. That row is a counterexample, and it is the same row that told a conditional apart from its converse.

steps.headline: A sound argument is valid and has only true premises

lead.text: Validity answers only the first of two questions about an argument. The second is whether its premises are true, and for that we need another word. We call an argument **sound** when it is valid and every one of its premises is true. A sound argument is the real prize, because validity carries the truth of the premises across to the conclusion, so the conclusion is guaranteed to be true. The whale argument is valid but not sound, since its first premise is false.

afterFigure.text: An argument can therefore go wrong in two separate ways. It can be invalid, so that its conclusion doesn't follow even if everything it says is *granted*, or it can be valid but unsound, so that the reasoning is fine but it starts from something false. When you meet a conclusion you believe to be false, ask which has happened. If you know the argument is valid, **one of its premises must be false**. And an unsound argument has not shown its conclusion to be *false*; it has only failed to give us a reason to accept it.

diagram.alt: A grid with validity across the top and the truth of the premises down the side. Only the cell where the argument is valid and every premise is true is sound, and it guarantees a true conclusion. A valid argument with a false premise is unsound and guarantees nothing. An invalid argument gives no guarantee either way.

blocks.text: Here is an argument: all mammals live on land; whales are mammals; therefore whales live on land. Is it a good argument? Most people say no at once, because the conclusion is plainly false, and yet a logician would tell you that the reasoning in it is faultless. The disagreement comes from two different questions that everyday speech runs together, and keeping them apart is among the most useful habits this course can give you.

To pull the questions apart we need a precise name for each, and a way of testing the first that doesn't depend on whether we happen to know the facts. Both are things we already have the tools for, since the truth tables of the last lessons are all the equipment that the test needs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test whether a conclusion follows, find the case that refutes it, and judge separately whether the premises are true.
intro.whyItMatters: A conclusion can be false because the reasoning is bad or because a premise is, and knowing which tells you what to challenge.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when its conclusion must be true if its premises are, and sound when it is valid and its premises really are true.

blocks.text: We call an argument **valid** when no row of the table makes every premise true and the conclusion false, and a single such row, a **counterexample**, is enough to show it invalid. We call it **sound** when it is valid *and* every premise is true, so a sound argument guarantees its conclusion. When you assess an argument, ask the two questions separately: does the conclusion follow, and are the premises true?

recap.nextHook: Next we use the test to name the two patterns of if-then reasoning that persuade without supporting, and the one that does.

lessons.title: Naming the fallacies

steps.headline: A rule tells us what its condition brings, not what else could bring the same result

lead.text: Take the rule “If it rains, the street is wet”, which we can write as p → q, with p for “It rains” and q for “The street is wet”. What it tells us is that whenever p holds, q holds as well. It does not say that p is the *only* way to reach q, and the figure shows why that matters: a street can be wet because a cleaner has just been along it, or because a pipe has burst, and neither of those makes the rule false.

afterFigure.text: So when we find the street wet, we are looking at the consequent and trying to run the rule backwards, from q to p. That is the move the [[converse|The conditional with its parts swapped: q → p. Met in 'Converse and contrapositive'.]] invites, and we saw in an earlier lesson that a rule can't be used that way, because the converse is a different claim. **What the rule gives us is a route from rain to a wet street, and nothing about the way back.**

lead.text: Put the rule to work on the wet street.

steps.headline: Arguing from q back to p is a fallacy, called affirming the consequent

lead.text: The pattern we have just been tempted by is “p → q; q; therefore p”. Its second premise asserts, or *affirms*, the consequent q, and from that it concludes the antecedent p, so we call it **affirming the consequent**. It is invalid, as the test of the last lesson will show in a moment, and it belongs to a larger family. A pattern of reasoning that persuades without really supporting its conclusion is a **fallacy**.

It persuades because the rule seems to fit the situation so neatly: the street is wet, which is just what the rule says rain would produce. But fitting is not the same as following. The test asks only whether a row exists with true premises and a false conclusion, and for this pattern it does.
Find the row that refutes “p → q; q; therefore p”, with p for “It rains” and q for “The street is wet”.

reveal.text: In the row with p false and q true, the street is wet because the cleaner has been, so the rule holds, the second premise holds, and it did not rain.

steps.headline: The mirror pattern, arguing from not-p to not-q, fails in the same way

lead.text: There is a second pattern that looks equally natural: “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”. It didn't rain, so the street isn't wet. This time the second premise denies the antecedent, and we call the pattern **denying the antecedent**. It fails for the *same* reason as before: a street that hasn't had rain on it can still be wet, since the rule never said that rain is the only cause.

There is a connection to the last two lessons worth making. Negating both parts of a conditional without swapping them gives ¬p → ¬q, which we saw is neither the converse nor the [[contrapositive|The conditional with its parts swapped and both negated: ¬q → ¬p. It says the same as the original. Met in 'Converse and contrapositive'.]] of the rule. Denying the antecedent treats that different claim as though it followed from the rule, and it doesn't. The [[counterexample|A row where every premise is true and the conclusion is false. It shows an argument is invalid. Met in 'Valid but untrue'.]] is the same row as before, with p false and q true.
Check the second fallacy against the same row, with p false and q true.

steps.headline: Running a rule backwards through its contrapositive is safe: that is modus tollens

lead.text: There is a way of arguing backwards from a rule that cannot go wrong. If the street is dry, it did not rain, because rain would have made it wet. In letters this is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p”: the rule, the denial of its consequent, and the denial of its antecedent. If p were true, the rule would force q, and q is false, so p *cannot* be true.

This is the contrapositive at work, and it is called **modus tollens**, from the Latin for “the mode that denies”. Its better-known sibling is “p → q; p; therefore q”, which reasons forwards from the condition and is called modus ponens. Both are valid, and the two fallacies are what you get by running them the wrong way round: **affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are modus ponens and modus tollens turned back to front**.

steps.headline: If the sensor overheats its light comes on, and the light is off

lead.text: Here is the safe direction used on a rule you can picture, with each step of the supposing written out.

workedSteps.text: Take the rule “If the sensor overheats, its warning light comes on”, and suppose we find the light off. Suppose the sensor had overheated. Then the rule would require the light to be on.
workedSteps.math: Then the light would be on

workedSteps.text: But the light is off, so the supposition cannot be right. The sensor did not overheat.
In letters, with p for overheating and q for the light being on, we started from the rule and the denial of its consequent, and ended with the denial of its antecedent.

lead.text: Now run the test of the last lesson on this pattern, “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p”.

reveal.text: The only row in which both p → q and ¬q are true is the one with p false and q false, and ¬p is true there. There is no counterexample.

steps.headline: Not every fallacy is a pattern of if-then: some change the subject

lead.text: Some fallacies can't be caught by a truth table, because what goes wrong is not the shape of the reasoning but the topic. Take “Their calculation must be wrong, because they are rude.” The conclusion is about a calculation, and the premise is about the person who made it. Rudeness has no bearing on arithmetic, since a rude person may calculate correctly and a polite one may not, so the premise gives no reason at all to accept the conclusion. We call this **attacking the person**.

The remedy follows from what an argument is. To answer one, examine its reasoning: look for a premise that is false, a step that doesn't follow, or a premise that has been left out. The character of the speaker matters only when the claim is *about* the speaker, as when we ask whether a witness was in the room, and that is not the case here.
Here is a fallacy of the second kind, and a choice of replies to it.

blocks.text: Here is a rule that nobody doubts: if it has rained, the street is wet. This morning you step outside and find the street wet. Did it rain? Many people feel a strong pull towards yes, and the pull is strong enough that arguments of exactly this shape persuade people in every walk of life.

The shape has a name, and so do two others. One persuades without supporting, a second is its mirror image and fails in the same way, and a third looks almost identical but is completely secure. Telling them apart needs a test, and we already have it from the last lesson: a search for a row in which the premises are true and the conclusion is false.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the two common fallacies of if-then reasoning, refute each with one row, and spot the valid pattern beside them.
intro.whyItMatters: These patterns turn up in everyday arguments, and naming them lets you say exactly what has gone wrong.

recap.keyIdea: Reasoning from q back to p, or from not-p to not-q, is invalid, while reasoning from not-q to not-p is valid.

blocks.text: A **fallacy** is a pattern of reasoning that persuades without supporting. Of the four ways of using “p → q; …”, two are fallacies, **affirming the consequent** and **denying the antecedent**, and each has a counterexample in the row where p is false and q is true. The other two are valid, and **modus tollens**, which runs from ¬q to ¬p, is the contrapositive at work. Fallacies such as **attacking the person** change the subject, and the answer to them is to examine the reasoning.
