questions.prompt: A claim is false. Is its negation true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Apply negation to the false claim.
Negation never leaves the value alone.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation of a false claim is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. Negation reverses the value, so the negation of a false claim is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Negation never leaves the value alone. Ask what ¬ does to a claim.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q false?
hints: Which case has the code correct and the door doing the wrong thing?
A conditional is only broken when what it asks for fails to happen.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p true and q false: the code is right and the door stays shut.

questions.onCorrect: That is the code being right and the door staying shut, the one case where the rule demands something and doesn't get it.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the code is wrong, so the rule has no demand on the door to break.
Here the code is wrong too. The rule only said something about correct codes.

questions.prompt: Of the four combinations of p and q, how many make p → q true?
hints: Start by finding the combination that breaks the rule.
There are four combinations in all.
Take away the ones that make it false and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only p true with q false makes it false, so the other three combinations make it true.

questions.onCorrect: Three. Only one combination breaks the rule, so the other three leave it true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of false cases. The question asks for the true ones.
One combination does break a rule. Find it and take it away.
Count the combinations where p is false as well as those where p is true. Only one breaks the rule.

questions.prompt: p is “The access code is correct” and q is “The door opens”, and both are false. Is p → q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is the code correct in this case?
A rule about correct codes can't be broken by a wrong code.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: True: p is false, so the rule is not broken.

questions.onCorrect: True. With a wrong code the rule isn't tested, so nothing breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule only said something about correct codes. Does a wrong code with a shut door break that?

questions.prompt: p is “The shape is a square” and q is “The shape has four sides”. For a four-sided rectangle that isn't a square, is p → q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is p true for this shape?
A rule about squares can't be broken by a shape that isn't one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: True: p is false, so the conditional is not broken.

questions.onCorrect: True. The shape isn't a square, so the rule about squares is untouched. A true q doesn't make p true.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false for this shape. A rule about squares can't be broken by a shape that isn't one.

questions.prompt: p is true and q is false. Is p → q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: Is the condition met in this case?
Does q deliver what p called for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False: p true with q false is the one breaking case.

questions.onCorrect: False. The antecedent holds and the consequent fails, the one case that breaks a conditional.

misconceptions.feedback: p holds, so the conditional is being tested. Does q deliver what p called for?

questions.prompt: Of the four combinations of p and q, how many make p → q false?
hints: A false conditional needs its condition met and its result missing.
List the four combinations of p and q.
Count those where p is true and q is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only p true with q false breaks a conditional, so one combination makes it false.

questions.onCorrect: One: p true and q false. Every other combination leaves the conditional true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many cases are true. Count the false ones.
A false conditional needs p true and q false together. How many combinations do that?
A rule can be broken. Find the combination that breaks it.

questions.prompt: Is q → p true or false when q is true and p is false? Answer with one word.
hints: In q → p, which part is the antecedent?
Is q true and p false a case with a true antecedent and a false consequent?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False: q → p has a true antecedent and a false consequent.

questions.onCorrect: False. In q → p the antecedent q holds and the consequent p fails. p → q is true in this same case.

misconceptions.feedback: In q → p, q comes first. Apply the rule from the last lesson with q as the antecedent.

questions.prompt: Across the four combinations of p and q, in how many do p → q and its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p take different truth values?
hints: Look back at the four rows of the worked example.
In each row, were the two values the same or different?
Count the rows in which they were different.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two take the same value in every combination, so there are none.

questions.onCorrect: None. The two have the same truth value in every case, so the contrapositive says the same thing.

misconceptions.feedback: The false case is false in both. Count the cases where they disagree.
Check each case against the matching one for ¬q → ¬p. They fail in the same case.
They don't disagree everywhere. Compare them case by case.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q true but its converse q → p false?
hints: The converse is false only when q is true and p is false.
Check that p → q is still true in that case.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true, p → q is true and q → p is false.

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true. The original holds, the converse fails, so the two are not the same claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Both are true here. You need a case where they disagree.
Here p → q is already false. You need it true.

questions.prompt: Choose the contrapositive of “If a parcel is fragile, it is labelled”.
hints: Swap the parts, then negate both.
The new antecedent is the negation of the old consequent.

acceptedIdeas: If a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile.

choices.label: If a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile.
If a parcel is labelled, it is fragile.
If a parcel is not fragile, it is not labelled.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if a parcel is not labelled, it is not fragile. It says the same as the original.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but doesn't negate them. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. It isn't the contrapositive.

questions.prompt: Relative to p → q, what is q → p called? Answer with one word.
hints: It swaps the two parts and negates nothing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The converse.

questions.onCorrect: The converse. The parts are swapped and nothing is negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The contrapositive also negates both parts. Here they are only swapped.

questions.prompt: Relative to p → q, what is ¬q → ¬p called? Answer with one word.
hints: The parts are swapped and both are negated.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive.

questions.onCorrect: The contrapositive. The parts are swapped and both are negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The converse only swaps the parts. Here both are negated as well.

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” If Ada is a knight, is Ben a knight or a knave? Answer with one word.
hints: A knight's sentence is true.
If it is true that Ben is a knave, what is Ben?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben is a knave, because a knight's statement is true.

questions.onCorrect: Knave. A knight's sentence is true, so Ada's claim about Ben has to hold.

misconceptions.feedback: Ada says Ben is a knave. If Ada always tells the truth, what does that make Ben?

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” How many of the four assignments fit her statement?
hints: Test the four assignments one at a time against what Ada says.
If Ada is a knight, her sentence must be true. If she is a knave, it must be false.
Count the assignments in which nobody breaks their rule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ada a knight with Ben a knave fits, and Ada a knave with Ben a knight fits. Ada and Ben both knights, and both knaves, do not, so two assignments fit.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Ada truthful with Ben a knave, or Ada lying with Ben a knight. One statement can leave several.

misconceptions.feedback: You found one assignment. Now assume Ada is a knave, and see whether Ben can have a kind that fits.
Some of the four assignments make Ada break her own rule. Cross those out.
The statement can be made to fit. Try each kind for Ada in turn.

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave,” and Ben says, “Ada and I are the same kind.” Is Ada a knight or a knave? Answer with one word.
hints: Ada's sentence leaves two assignments. Test Ben's sentence against each.
In the assignment where Ada is a knave, Ben is a knight. Is his sentence true?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ada is a knight and Ben a knave.

questions.onCorrect: Knight. Ben's sentence is false in the only assignment that survives, which makes him a knave and Ada the knight.

misconceptions.feedback: If Ada were a knave, Ben would be a knight. Would Ben's sentence be true then?

questions.prompt: Cara says, “Drew is a knight,” and Drew says, “Cara is a knave.” How many of the four assignments fit both statements?
hints: Test each of the four assignments against both statements.
In each assignment, check that Cara and Drew each obey their own kind.
Count the assignments in which nobody breaks a rule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Cara and Drew both knights fails on Drew's sentence, a knight Cara with a knave Drew fails on Cara's, a knave Cara with a knight Drew fails on Cara's, and both knaves fails on Drew's, so none fit.

questions.onCorrect: None. Every assignment makes someone break their rule, so no assignment survives.

misconceptions.feedback: Check your assignment against both statements. Does each speaker obey their own kind?
Test each assignment against both statements. Both speakers have to obey their kind.

questions.prompt: Ada is a knave and says, “Ben is a knave.” Is Ben a knight or a knave? Answer with one word.
hints: A knave's sentence is false.
If “Ben is a knave” is false, what is Ben?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben is a knight.

questions.onCorrect: Knight. A knave's sentence is false, so Ben is not a knave.

misconceptions.feedback: A knave lies. What does that do to what Ada says about Ben?

questions.prompt: For two people who could each be a knight or a knave, how many assignments should you test?
hints: Count the choices for Ada, then the choices for Ben.
Every choice for Ada pairs with each choice for Ben.
Multiply the two numbers of choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of two people has two possible kinds, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 assignments.

questions.onCorrect: Four: 2 × 2. Every choice for Ada pairs with both choices for Ben.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of choices for one person. Pair each of Ada's with each of Ben's.
Pair every one of Ada's choices with every one of Ben's. Count the pairs.

questions.prompt: How many different states can the two lamps be in?
hints: List the states for lamp 1 on, then for lamp 1 off.
With lamp 1 on, lamp 2 can be on or off. The same is true with lamp 1 off.
Count the states in the two lists together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lamp 1 has two settings and lamp 2 has two, so the states number 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Four: 2 × 2. Every setting of one lamp pairs with both settings of the other.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the settings of one lamp. The second lamp doubles it.
Check the list. Both lamps on is one state, so what are the others?

questions.prompt: In how many of the four rows is p ∧ q true?
hints: Check the rows one at a time.
In which row are p and q both true?
Count the rows that satisfy that.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: “p and q” needs both claims true, and only the row with p and q both true has that, so there is one row.

questions.onCorrect: One. “p and q” needs both, and only the first row has both.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what you get if one true claim is enough. ∧ needs both.
Check a row with only one claim true. Does “p and q” hold there?
Go through the four rows one at a time and test “p and q”.

questions.prompt: In how many of the four rows is p ∨ q true?
hints: Which rows have at least one true claim?
The inclusive “or” also holds when both are true.
Find the one row that fails and take it from four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inclusive “or” fails only when both claims are false, so it holds in the other three rows.

questions.onCorrect: Three. “p or q” holds unless both are false, and the inclusive reading counts the row where both are true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many rows make p ∧ q true. Here one true claim is enough.
Rows where both claims are true count too, because ∨ is inclusive.
The row where both claims are false fails.

questions.prompt: Someone reasons: “p or q is true, and p is true, so q must be false.” Which row shows that the reasoning goes wrong?
hints: Look for a row where both facts hold.
In that row, is q false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p true, q true: both facts hold, yet q is true.

questions.onCorrect: In the row with p true and q true, both facts hold and q is still true. One such row is enough to break the reasoning.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false here, so one of the starting facts fails. Keep only rows where both facts hold.
p ∨ q is false here, so this row isn't a case the reasoning starts from.

questions.prompt: Three independent claims each have two truth values. How many rows does their table need?
hints: Two claims need four rows.
A third claim can be true or false in each of those rows.
Double the four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each claim doubles the number of rows, so three claims give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 rows.

questions.onCorrect: Eight: 2 × 2 × 2. Each new claim doubles the rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the choices. Each claim multiplies the cases instead.
That is the rows for two claims. The third claim doubles them.

questions.prompt: Can inclusive p ∨ q be true when both claims are true? Answer yes or no.
hints: The inclusive “or” needs at least one claim true.
Does “at least one” allow two?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes: at least one is true when both are.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. The inclusive “or” needs at least one claim true, and both counts.

misconceptions.feedback: The inclusive “or” doesn't rule out both. What does “inclusive” add?

questions.prompt: “If the battery is charged, the torch lights. The battery is charged. Therefore the torch lights.” Is “The torch lights” a premise or a conclusion? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim does the word “therefore” introduce?
Is “The torch lights” offered as support, or is it what the others support?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Conclusion: it follows “therefore”.

questions.onCorrect: Conclusion. The first two sentences are the support, and “therefore” introduces what they support.

misconceptions.feedback: A premise is offered as support. Is “The torch lights” offered to support something, or supported by something?

questions.prompt: In how many of the four rows are both p → q and p true?
hints: Test p first. Which rows have p true?
In those rows, is p → q true?
Count the rows that pass both tests.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both premises hold only when p is true and p → q is true, and that happens only in the row with p true and q true, so there is one row.

questions.onCorrect: One. Only the first row makes both premises true, and q is true in that row.

misconceptions.feedback: Two rows have p true. Is p → q true in both?
Both premises have to hold in the same row. Test p first.
Go through the four rows and test both premises in each.

questions.prompt: “The torch lights, because the battery is charged and a charged battery makes it light.” In this passage, is “The battery is charged” a premise or a conclusion? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim does “because” introduce?
Is the battery being charged what the speaker wants you to accept, or a reason for it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Premise: it follows “because”.

questions.onCorrect: Premise. It is offered as a reason for the torch lighting, though it comes later in the passage.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage starts with its conclusion. Is the battery being charged what the speaker wants you to accept, or a reason for it?

questions.prompt: “Either the parcel is at the desk or it is in the locker. It is not at the desk. Therefore it is in the locker.” Which location is the conclusion: desk or locker? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim follows “therefore”?
The two earlier claims are offered to support one claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The locker claim is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Locker. “Therefore” introduces it, and the two earlier claims support it.

misconceptions.feedback: The desk appears in the premises. Which claim comes after “therefore”?

questions.prompt: What do we call a claim offered as support for a conclusion? Answer with one word.
hints: It is one of the reasons in an argument.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A premise.

questions.onCorrect: A premise. It supports the conclusion; it is not what the argument wants you to accept.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion is what the support is for. What is the support called?

questions.prompt: In “p → q; p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion? Answer with one letter.
hints: Which claim follows “therefore”?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: q is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: q. It follows “therefore”, and the two earlier statements are offered as its support.

misconceptions.feedback: p appears in the premises. Which letter follows “therefore”?

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; p; therefore q” valid or invalid? Answer with one word.
hints: Look for a row where both premises are true and q is false.
Which row has both p → q and p true?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid: no row has true premises and a false conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. In every row where both premises hold, q holds too.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and q is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: How many counterexamples may a valid argument have?
hints: Validity says no case has true premises and a false conclusion.
What does the definition allow for such cases?
Count the exceptions it permits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A single counterexample would make it invalid, so a valid argument has none.

questions.onCorrect: None. One counterexample would make the argument invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: One counterexample is enough to make an argument invalid. How many does validity permit?
Validity is a guarantee over every case. How many exceptions does that allow?

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; q; therefore p” valid or invalid? Answer with one word.
hints: Try the row where p is false and q is true.
Are both premises true there, and what happens to the conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: p false and q true is a counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. With p false and q true, both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the row with p false and q true. Do both premises hold, and what happens to p?

questions.prompt: A valid argument contains a false premise. Is it sound or unsound? Answer with one word.
hints: Soundness asks for something about the premises as well as validity.
What does a false premise do to that?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Unsound: one premise is false.

questions.onCorrect: Unsound. Soundness needs every premise to be true as well as validity.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity alone isn't enough. What does soundness also ask of the premises?

questions.prompt: A valid argument has all true premises. Is it sound or unsound? Answer with one word.
hints: Soundness needs validity and true premises.
Does this argument have both?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sound: valid, with every premise true.

questions.onCorrect: Sound. It is valid and every premise is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Soundness needs validity and true premises. Does this argument have both?

questions.prompt: How many cases with true premises and a false conclusion does it take to show that an argument is invalid?
hints: Validity promises that there are none.
How many exceptions break a promise of none?
Count the cases needed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Validity promises there is no such case, so a single one shows that the argument is invalid.

questions.onCorrect: One. A single case with true premises and a false conclusion refutes validity.

misconceptions.feedback: With no such case, the argument is valid. How many are needed to refute it?
You don't need several. Validity promises there are none.

questions.prompt: Which case refutes “p → q; q; therefore p”?
hints: A refuting case has both premises true and the conclusion false.
The conclusion is p. In which case is p false while both premises hold?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p false and q true: both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true: both premises hold and p is false. A true consequent doesn't establish its antecedent.

misconceptions.feedback: Here p is true, so the conclusion holds. You need a case where it fails.
Here q is false, so a premise fails. Keep both premises true.

questions.prompt: Take p false and q true in “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”. Is the conclusion ¬q true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: q is true in this row.
What does ¬ do to a true claim?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False: q is true, so ¬q is false.

questions.onCorrect: False. Both premises hold but ¬q fails, so denying the antecedent is invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion is ¬q, and q is true here. What does negation do to it?

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p” valid or invalid? Answer with one word.
hints: Find the rows where both p → q and ¬q are true.
Is ¬p true in every one of them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid: it is modus tollens.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. If p were true, p → q would force q, but ¬q says otherwise. This is modus tollens.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p → q and ¬q are true and ¬p is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: Someone argues, “Their calculation must be wrong, because they are rude.” Which response examines the reasoning?
hints: Which reply deals with the calculation itself?
Does the speaker's manner tell us anything about the arithmetic?

acceptedIdeas: Check the disputed calculation step by step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Check the disputed calculation itself.

choices.label: Check the disputed calculation step by step
Treat the speaker's popularity as proof

questions.onCorrect: Check the step itself. Rudeness doesn't make a calculation right or wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That attacks the person again. It doesn't test the calculation.
Popularity is not evidence about the calculation either.

questions.prompt: In “p → q; q; therefore p”, which part is affirmed: the antecedent or the consequent? Answer with one word.
hints: The second premise asserts one letter.
Is that letter before or after the arrow?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The consequent, q.

questions.onCorrect: Consequent. The argument asserts q, the part after the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback: The antecedent is p, before the arrow. Which letter does the second premise assert?

questions.prompt: In “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”, which part is denied: the antecedent or the consequent? Answer with one word.
hints: The second premise negates one letter.
Is that letter before or after the arrow?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The antecedent, p.

questions.onCorrect: Antecedent. ¬p denies p, the part before the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback: The consequent is q, and the second premise denies p. Which part is that?

questions.prompt: Why do we throw away the rows where p is true?
hints: Which fact have we just added?
A row stays only if it fits everything we know.

acceptedIdeas: We were told p is false, so those rows don't fit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: We were told p is false, so rows with p true do not fit.

choices.label: We were told p is false, so those rows don't fit.
p ∨ q is false in those rows.
Rows with p true are always wrong.

questions.onCorrect: The rows must match everything we know. We know p is false, so those rows are out.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the rows with p true. Is p ∨ q false in them?
A row with p true is fine in general. It just doesn't match what we were told here.

questions.prompt: An alarm rings if sensor p or sensor q is triggered. Of the four settings of the two sensors, how many leave the alarm silent?
hints: The alarm rings when p ∨ q is true.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The alarm is silent only when neither sensor is triggered, which is one setting.

questions.onCorrect: One: neither sensor triggered. “p or q” fails only when both are false.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many settings ring the alarm. Count the silent ones.
A setting with one sensor triggered still rings the alarm.
Go through the four settings one at a time and check the alarm.

questions.prompt: Which list is a complete table for two claims?
hints: Each claim can be true or false, and every pairing needs a row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every pairing appears once: TT, TF, FT, FF.

questions.onCorrect: Every pairing of true and false appears exactly once, so the table is complete.

misconceptions.feedback: One pairing is missing. Pair each value of p with both values of q.
One row appears twice, and another pairing is missing.

questions.prompt: A café sign says “Tea or coffee included.” Dev takes both. In the logician's sense, is the sign's claim true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Does the symbol ∨ rule out the case where both hold?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The logician's “or” allows both.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. In logic “or” includes both, so taking both still makes it true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the everyday reading. The logician's “or” doesn't rule out both.

questions.prompt: Is the file encrypted?
hints: The rule says what encrypted files need. Does it say only encrypted files need one?
Could a file need a key for some other reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily. Other files may need a key too.

questions.onCorrect: Not necessarily. “If encrypted, then key” doesn't say that a key means encrypted. Turning a rule round changes it.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule says what encrypted files need. It doesn't say that only encrypted files need one.
The rule doesn't rule encryption out. It just doesn't settle it.

questions.prompt: Why is ¬q → ¬p false in the row where p is true and q is false?
hints: Work out ¬q and ¬p for this row.
What makes any conditional false?

acceptedIdeas: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: a true antecedent with a false consequent.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ¬q is true and ¬p is false, so it has a true antecedent and a false consequent.

choices.label: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: a true antecedent with a false consequent.
Swapping the parts never changes a conditional.
A negated claim is always false.

questions.onCorrect: ¬q is true and ¬p is false, which is the same breaking pattern as in p → q, reached by swapping and negating.

misconceptions.feedback: Swapping alone does change a conditional, which is why the converse differs. Look at ¬q and ¬p.
¬ flips a value. It doesn't fix it.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If it's a square, it has four sides.” A shape does not have four sides. What follows?
hints: Form the contrapositive of the rule.
The contrapositive starts from exactly this fact.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is not a square, by the contrapositive.

questions.onCorrect: It is not a square. The contrapositive says the same as the rule: no four sides, so not a square.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs against the rule: squares have four sides.
The rule's contrapositive starts from exactly this fact.

questions.prompt: What is the converse of “If it rains, the match is cancelled”?
hints: The converse swaps the two parts and negates nothing.
Which part is the antecedent, and where does it go?

acceptedIdeas: If the match is cancelled, it rains.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If the match is cancelled, it rains.

choices.label: If the match is cancelled, it rains.
If it doesn't rain, the match isn't cancelled.
If it rains, the match is played.

questions.onCorrect: The converse swaps the parts and negates nothing: if the match is cancelled, it rains.

misconceptions.feedback: That negates both parts but keeps the order. The converse only swaps.
That keeps the order and negates one part. The converse only swaps the parts.

questions.prompt: What is the contrapositive of “If it rains, the match is cancelled”?
hints: Swap the parts, then negate both.

acceptedIdeas: If the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap and negate both parts: if the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.

choices.label: If the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.
If the match is cancelled, it rains.
If it doesn't rain, the match isn't cancelled.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but negates neither. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. The contrapositive also swaps them.

questions.prompt: Which claim is Sam trying to get you to accept: the umbrella or the forecast? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim is the reason, and which is the thing the reason is for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sam wants you to take an umbrella. The forecast is the reason given.

questions.onCorrect: Taking an umbrella is what Sam wants. The forecast is offered as the reason.

misconceptions.feedback: Sam gives the forecast as a reason. What is it a reason for?

questions.prompt: “It will rain, so the match is off.” Which claim is the conclusion: the rain or the match? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim follows the word “so”?
Which claim is the other one offered to support?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The match: “so” introduces it.

questions.onCorrect: The match is off. The rain is the reason given, and it is meant to support the match being off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reason given. What does it support?

questions.prompt: Why isn't “the last train is at nine” the conclusion, even though it comes last?
hints: Ask what the claim is doing for the others.
Does it tell us what the speaker wants accepted, or why?

acceptedIdeas: Position doesn't decide; it supports the claim that we must leave.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position does not decide: the claim supports the conclusion that we must leave.

choices.label: Position doesn't decide; it supports the claim that we must leave.
The last sentence is never a conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Where a claim sits doesn't decide its role. It is a premise because it supports the claim that we must leave.

misconceptions.feedback: A conclusion can come last. Here it just doesn't.
“Because” introduces a reason, which is a premise.

questions.prompt: “Since the shop is shut on Sundays and today is Sunday, you can't buy bread today.” Which claim is the conclusion?
hints: Which claim are the others offered to support?
“Since” introduces reasons.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You can't buy bread today.

choices.label: The shop is shut on Sundays.

questions.onCorrect: You can't buy bread today. “Since” introduces the two premises that support it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a reason offered after “since”. What does it help to support?
That follows “since”, so it is a reason. Which claim does it support?

questions.prompt: Did Sam break his promise? Answer yes or no.
hints: Who was the promise about: people who passed, or people who failed?
What would Sam have to do to be caught out?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The promise only covered the case where you passed.

questions.onCorrect: No. Sam only promised something about passing. A kind act in another case can't break it.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at what the promise covers. Is it about people who failed?

questions.prompt: In “The door opens if the code is correct”, which part is the antecedent?
hints: Look for the word “if” and see what follows it.
The antecedent is the condition, wherever it stands in the sentence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The antecedent is the part after “if”: the code is correct.

questions.onCorrect: The antecedent is whatever follows “if”, so here it is the code being correct. “The door opens” is the consequent, though it comes first.

misconceptions.feedback: That part stands first, but it isn't the one after “if”. It is the consequent.
The antecedent is one part of the sentence, the part that sets the condition, and not the whole conditional.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the match being cancelled without rain break the promise?
hints: Read the promise again. Which days does it cover?

acceptedIdeas: The promise only speaks about rainy days.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The promise only speaks about rainy days, so a dry day can't break it.

choices.label: The promise only speaks about rainy days.
A cancelled match always keeps a promise.

questions.onCorrect: The promise covers only rainy days. On a dry day it says nothing, so it can't be broken.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule doesn't say rain is the only cause, or even a cause. It says what follows when it rains.
A cancelled match keeps this promise only on a rainy day. Dry days are not covered at all.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.” Which of these numbers would break it?
hints: To break the rule a number must meet the condition and miss the result.
Check each number: is it divisible by 4, and if so, is it even?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None: 8 is a multiple of 4 and is even, and 6 and 7 are not multiples of 4.

questions.onCorrect: None. Breaking the rule needs a multiple of 4 that is odd, and 8 is divisible by 4 and even.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 isn't divisible by 4, so the rule says nothing about it.
7 isn't divisible by 4, so the rule has no say about it.
8 is divisible by 4. Is it also even?

questions.prompt: Why is the assignment in which Eli and Fay are both knaves ruled out?
hints: Work out whether Eli's sentence is true when both are knaves.
A knave's sentences are all false.

acceptedIdeas: Eli is a knave, but his sentence is true when both are knaves.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eli's sentence is true when both are knaves, and a knave cannot say a true sentence.

choices.label: Eli is a knave, but his sentence is true when both are knaves.
Two knaves can't be on the island together.
Eli's sentence is false, and a knave can't say a false sentence.

questions.onCorrect: A knave's sentence has to be false. Here Eli's is true, so the assignment breaks a rule.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing stops two knaves from standing together. Check each person's statement against their kind.
A knave is supposed to say false things. Check whether Eli's sentence is false in this assignment.

questions.prompt: Gus says, “Hal is a knight.” Hal says, “Gus and I are different kinds.” Is Gus a knight or a knave? Answer with one word.
hints: List the four assignments for Gus and Hal.
Test each against both sentences. Which assignments survive?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Gus is a knave: only the assignment with both knaves survives.

questions.onCorrect: Knave. Only one assignment survives, both knaves, where each sentence is false as it must be.

misconceptions.feedback: If Gus were a knight, Hal would be a knight and Hal's sentence would have to be true. Is it?

questions.prompt: A knave says, “It is raining.” Is that claim true or false? Answer with one word.
hints: A knave never tells the truth.
Every sentence a knave says is false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: False: a knave's sentences are all false.

questions.onCorrect: False. A knave always lies, so whatever a knave says is false, even a sentence about the weather.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what a knight's sentence would be. What does a knave say?

questions.prompt: Does the street being wet prove that it rained? Answer yes or no.
hints: The rule says what rain does to the street.
Does it say that rain is the only thing that wets a street?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: the street could be wet for another reason.

questions.onCorrect: No. The rule says rain wets the street. It doesn't say that nothing else does.

misconceptions.feedback: Rain is one way to get a wet street. Does the rule say it is the only way?

questions.prompt: “If the sensor overheats, the light turns on. The light is on, so the sensor overheated.” Which part of the conditional is affirmed: antecedent or consequent?
hints: The antecedent follows “if”, and the consequent follows “then”.
Which part does the second sentence assert?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The light being on is the consequent.

questions.onCorrect: Consequent. The argument asserts the “then” part and argues back to the “if” part.

misconceptions.feedback: The antecedent is the “if” part, the overheating. The second sentence asserts the light being on.

questions.prompt: Why does the light being off show that the sensor didn't overheat?
hints: What does the rule say overheating does to the light?
What would we see if the sensor had overheated?

acceptedIdeas: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it didn't.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it is off.

choices.label: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it didn't.
The light is only on when nothing overheats.
Sensors that don't overheat keep their lights off.

questions.onCorrect: Overheating would have turned the light on. It is off, so the sensor didn't overheat.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the rule. It says what overheating does to the light.
The rule doesn't say that. It says what overheating does, not what happens without it.

questions.prompt: “If it's a bird, it has feathers. This animal has feathers, so it's a bird.” Is this reasoning valid or invalid? Answer with one word.
hints: Which part of the rule does the second sentence assert?
Does the rule say that only birds have feathers?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: it affirms the consequent.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. It affirms the consequent: feathers could come from another source, so the rule doesn't give the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule says what birds have. Does it say that only birds have feathers?

questions.prompt: If the first two sentences were true, would Ana have to be rich? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the first two sentences are true. What follows about Ana?
Ignore whether dragons exist.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A dragon owner is rich, and Ana owns one.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. If the premises held, Ana would have to be rich. Whether they hold is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Suppose the first two sentences are true, whatever the real world is like. Could Ana avoid being rich?

questions.prompt: All the premises of a valid argument are true. Must its conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion.
What does that leave when the premises are true?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes: validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion, so true premises force a true conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion. What does that leave?

questions.prompt: Why is one counterexample enough to show that an argument is invalid?
hints: What does validity say about cases with true premises and a false conclusion?
Does it allow some of them?

acceptedIdeas: Validity promises that there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validity promises there is no such case, so one case breaks the promise.

choices.label: Validity promises that there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
Most of the rows have to be counterexamples.
The premises are false in all the other rows.

questions.onCorrect: Validity is a promise about every case, so a single exception breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity allows no such case at all. It is not a matter of how many.
The other rows don't matter. Validity is about the cases with true premises.

questions.prompt: A learner says: “That's invalid, because the conclusion is false.” Is the learner right? Answer yes or no.
hints: Ask whether true premises would force the conclusion.
What does a false conclusion tell us about the premises?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: the argument is valid, and unsound because its first premise is false.

questions.onCorrect: No. The conclusion follows from the premises, so it is valid. The first premise is false, so it is unsound.

misconceptions.feedback: A false conclusion doesn't make an argument invalid. Ask whether true premises would force it.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q” valid or invalid? Answer with one word.
hints: Find the rows where both premises are true.
Is q true in every one of them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid: the only row with true premises has q true.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. The only row where both premises hold is the one with p false and q true, and q is true there.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p ∨ q and ¬p are both true and q is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: Who is right?
hints: Could the envelope hold a £10 note and not hold one?
Opening the envelope finds out what is inside. Does it change what is inside?

acceptedIdeas: Exactly one of them, but we don't know which yet.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exactly one of them. The envelope already holds a note or it doesn't.

choices.label: Exactly one of them, but we don't know which yet.

questions.onCorrect: One of them is right already. Not knowing which is a gap in us, not in the envelope. Logic starts there.

misconceptions.feedback: Opening the envelope finds out what is inside. It doesn't decide it.
Mia says the note is there and Jon says it isn't. The envelope can't match both.

questions.prompt: A jar holds some sweets and nobody has counted them. How many truth values does “The jar holds an even number of sweets” have right now?
hints: Does the jar hold some number of sweets right now?
Even or odd is already settled by what is in the jar.
In one case, how many verdicts does a claim get?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The jar holds some number, so the claim already has one value, even though no one knows it.

questions.onCorrect: One. The jar's contents settle it, whether or not anyone counts. Not knowing doesn't remove the value.

misconceptions.feedback: Not counting doesn't remove the verdict. The jar already holds some number.
Two verdicts exist, but the contents of the jar have already settled which applies.
“Unknown” describes the person who hasn't counted, not the claim.

questions.prompt: Nobody has opened the envelope. What does that tell us about Mia's claim?
hints: Does opening the envelope change what is inside it?

acceptedIdeas: It has a truth value already; we just haven't found it out.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The envelope already holds what it holds, so the claim already has a truth value.

choices.label: It has a truth value already; we just haven't found it out.
It has no truth value until someone looks.

questions.onCorrect: The envelope already holds what it holds, so the claim already has its truth value.

misconceptions.feedback: Looking finds out what is there. It doesn't put it there.
“Unknown” describes what we know. The claim is checked against the envelope, not against us.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the negation of “The door is open”?
hints: The negation claims that the original fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “The door is not open” says the original claim fails.

questions.onCorrect: The negation says the original fails: the door is not open.

misconceptions.feedback: That agrees with the original, with more emphasis. A negation says the original fails.
That asks. It doesn't claim that the original fails.

flashcards.front: When p is false, what truth value does ¬p have?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation is true.

flashcards.front: What kind of sentence is “Where is the key?”: claim, question or command?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a question.

flashcards.front: When is p → q false? Answer with the two values in order.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is true and q is false.

flashcards.front: Is p → q true or false when p is false and q is true?
flashcards.back: True: the rule is not broken.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The material conditional is true.

flashcards.front: Name the equivalent transformation of p → q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive is equivalent.

flashcards.front: How many assignments distinguish a conditional from its contrapositive?
flashcards.back: Zero: they agree on every assignment.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They differ on zero assignments.

flashcards.front: How many type assignments are possible for two islanders before any claims are checked?
flashcards.back: Four assignments: each islander has two possible types.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two times two gives four assignments.

flashcards.front: A knave says “Eli is a knight.” What is Eli’s type?
flashcards.back: Eli is a knave because the statement is false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eli must be a knave.

flashcards.front: How many rows does a complete truth table for four independent claims need?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four independent claims require sixteen assignments.

flashcards.front: When p and q are both true, is inclusive p ∨ q true or false?
flashcards.back: True: at least one is true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inclusive disjunction is true.

flashcards.front: What is a claim offered as support in an argument called?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a premise.

flashcards.front: For “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is q.

flashcards.front: A valid argument has one false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
flashcards.back: Unsound: soundness requires every premise to be true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The argument is unsound.

flashcards.front: How many counterexamples are compatible with validity?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Validity permits zero counterexamples.

flashcards.front: “p → q; q; therefore p” affirms which part of the conditional?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It affirms the consequent.

flashcards.front: Is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p” valid or invalid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The inference is valid.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two claims after 'because' are offered as support for the claim that the museum is closed.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If 9 is even, 9 is divisible by 2.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 9 is even.

question.prompt: How should this argument be classified?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its form is p implies q; p; therefore q, which is valid. The premise that 9 is even is false, so the argument is unsound.

choices.label: Invalid because the conclusion is false

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the router is offline, the page fails to load.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The router is online.

question.prompt: What is the gap in this argument?

acceptedIdeas: A different fault could still prevent loading.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This denies the antecedent. A true conditional allows an online router and a failed page; another fault can prevent loading.

choices.label: An online router guarantees every page loads.
A different fault could still prevent loading.
The first premise says the router is offline.

courseChecks.title: Bring it together
courseChecks.description: Use all eight lessons to test arguments and repair a mistaken inference. Results appear after the final response.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a project passed the audit, it received a certificate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This project received no certificate.

question.prompt: Assume the rule is true. A certificate was not issued. What follows?

acceptedIdeas: It did not pass the audit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If it had passed, it would have received a certificate. The missing certificate therefore rules out passing, but says nothing about whether an audit happened.

choices.label: It did not pass the audit.
Every uncertified project was never audited.

question.prompt: Across all four rows, how many make NOT (p AND q) true?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The conjunction is true only in the true–true row. Negating it makes each of the other three rows true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number inside is greater than 20.

question.prompt: A sealed envelope contains a number. You have not opened it. How should you treat notice A?

acceptedIdeas: It is a claim whose truth is currently unknown to you.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The notice asserts something about a fixed number. Not knowing whether it is true does not turn it into a command or remove its classical truth value.

choices.label: It is a claim whose truth is currently unknown to you.
It has no truth value until someone opens the envelope.
It is a command to choose a larger number.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a badge is active, the gate opens.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gate opens.

question.prompt: Which change repairs the inference while keeping its first premise?

acceptedIdeas: Replace the second premise with 'The gate does not open' and conclude 'The badge is not active'.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With the gate closed, an active badge would contradict the first premise. That repair uses the contrapositive; the other proposed patterns do not rule out other causes.

choices.label: Keep the second premise; all effects have one cause.
Replace the second premise with 'The gate does not open' and conclude 'The badge is not active'.
Replace the second premise with 'The badge is not active' and conclude 'The gate does not open'.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ivo: Mara is a knave.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mara: Ivo is a knave.

question.prompt: Knights tell the truth and knaves lie. How many type assignments satisfy both statements?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Exactly one speaker must be a knight. Ivo knight with Mara knave works, and the reverse works. Both-knight and both-knave assignments contradict their statements.

statements.label: A
statements.text: p implies q.

statements.label: B
statements.text: q is true.

question.prompt: Which assignment is a counterexample to this argument?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: When p is false and q is true, both premises are true and the conclusion p is false. One such assignment refutes validity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sample is in cabinet 4: it is either in cabinet 4 or cabinet 9, and cabinet 9 is empty.

question.prompt: Which sentence supplies the conclusion, even though it appears first?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The alternatives and the empty cabinet support the first claim, that the sample is in cabinet 4. Position alone does not identify a premise.

choices.label: The sample is in one of the two cabinets.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a package contains glass, it is marked G.

question.prompt: Which inspected package violates the stated implication?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The implication requires G for glass packages. It does not forbid G on other packages, so only glass without G violates it.

courseChecks.title: Use it a week later
courseChecks.description: Apply the ideas to new reports and decisions after a week. Each problem uses a fresh case.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Either valve A or valve B is leaking. Inspection ruled out A. That is why we will repair B: valve B is leaking.

question.prompt: Which claim is the conclusion of this maintenance report?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The alternatives and the inspection result are used to establish that B leaks. The proposed repair is motivated by that conclusion.

choices.label: At least one valve is leaking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Record the room temperature.

question.prompt: Which version makes the instruction into a claim?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The last version asserts that recording occurred. It can be true or false; the alternatives remain a question and an instruction.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Premise A has been checked and is true.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Premise B has been checked and is true.

question.prompt: Both listed premises are true. What else is needed before calling the argument sound?

acceptedIdeas: There must be no case with both premises true and the conclusion false.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Soundness requires true premises and a valid inference. Validity excludes every true-premise, false-conclusion case.

choices.label: There must be no case with both premises true and the conclusion false.
The conclusion must be written after the premises.

question.prompt: A safety rule says: if the door is open, the warning lamp is on. The door is closed and the lamp is on. What does this show?

acceptedIdeas: The observation respects the rule; it does not establish what caused the light.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rule constrains cases with an open door. A closed door with a lit lamp does not violate it or identify the cause of the light.

choices.label: The observation respects the rule; it does not establish what caused the light.
The lamp proves the door is actually open.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lena says a forecast follows from the measurements.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A colleague objects that Lena is usually impatient.

question.prompt: Which review directly tests the reasoning?

acceptedIdeas: Check whether the measurements support the forecast.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inspect the link between the measurements and forecast. A remark about Lena's temperament supplies no counterexample or faulty calculation.

choices.label: Count how many people dislike Lena.
Check whether the measurements support the forecast.
Reject the forecast because impatience is undesirable.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Published implies passed review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This report did not pass review.

question.prompt: Assume every published report passed review. A report did not pass review. Which conclusion follows?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This uses the contrapositive. Publishing would require a passed review; the rule says nothing about whether drafting happened.

choices.label: The report has never been drafted.

question.prompt: How many assignments make p AND (q OR NOT q) true? Use the four rows shown.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: q OR NOT q is true in every classical row. The whole expression is therefore true exactly in the two rows where p is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rui: We are different types.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sol: Rui tells the truth.

question.prompt: Each witness either always tells the truth or always lies. Which types fit these reports?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sol's report requires the same truth-telling status for both. Then Rui's claim that their types differ is false. Rui lies, and Sol's report is false too.

choices.label: Rui tells the truth; Sol lies
Rui lies; Sol tells the truth
